e.etymology: The Italian form of Guinevere, King Arthur's queen, from Welsh Gwenhwyfar, made of gwen, white or fair, and a word for phantom or spirit. Jennifer is the Cornish form of the same name.
namesakes: Ginny Weasley (Harry Potter character, in full Ginevra)

assoc.t: Ginevra, Ginny Weasley's full name in Harry Potter

e.meaning: prosperous, thriving; also read as princess
e.etymology: A feminine form of Aamir, from Arabic amir with a long first vowel, prosperous or full of life. Many families use it as a spelling of Amira, princess, the feminine of amir, commander.
A modern elaboration of Sarai, the first name of the biblical Sarah, with the -iya ending; it also sits close to Soraya.
A modern feminine name built on Dan- names such as Daniel and Danielle with the -ylah ending of Nylah and Kylah.
A spelling of Nola, a name of mixed background: a short form of Finola, the Irish Fionnuala, and of Magnolia, and sometimes a feminine form of Nolan.

assoc.t: NOLA, the nickname for New Orleans, Louisiana

e.etymology: A respelling of Jackson, the English surname meaning son of Jack. Jack began as a medieval pet form of John.
A form of Azarias, the Greek and Latin spelling of the Hebrew name Azariah, God has helped, given the -ius ending of Darius and Cassius.
A respelling of Maverick. The word comes from Samuel Maverick, a 19th-century Texas rancher whose unbranded cattle were called mavericks, and came to mean anyone who goes their own way.

assoc.t: Tom Cruise's pilot call sign in Top Gun, spelled Maverick

e.etymology: A spelling of Analia, a Spanish combination of Ana and Lía, influenced by Aliyah.
An English surname used as a first name. Its best-known bearer is Nashville's Ryman Auditorium, the longtime home of the Grand Ole Opry, named for riverboat captain Thomas Ryman.

assoc.t: Ryman Auditorium, Nashville home of the Grand Ole Opry

e.etymology: An Indian boys' name that matches the Sanskrit word prayana, a setting out or journey.
A recent American coinage in the Zy- family with Zyon, Zylen and Zyaire.
A Yiddish pet form of Devorah (Deborah), Hebrew for bee, reflecting the Hasidic pronunciation Dvoira. It is used almost entirely in Hasidic Jewish communities.
Origin uncertain. Fiction has used it twice: Dr. Zira, the chimpanzee scientist of Planet of the Apes, and Zira, the villain of The Lion King II.

assoc.t: Zira, the villain lioness of The Lion King II

e.etymology: A modern name that reshapes Lennon around Lynn; Lennon is an Irish surname made famous by John Lennon.
A spelling of Mayla, a modern name that joins May to the -la ending of Kayla and Layla.
From the Old English personal name Saegar, made of sae, sea, and gar, spear, which survived as a surname. Baseball's Corey Seager has raised its profile.
namesakes: Corey Seager (two-time World Series MVP shortstop)

e.etymology: Anori is the Greenlandic word for wind and a given name in Greenland. In the US it also fits the sound pattern of Amari, Amori and Anaya.
Created for Neteyam, the eldest son of Jake Sully and Neytiri in James Cameron's Avatar: The Way of Water (2022). It is a name in the film's invented Na'vi language.

assoc.t: eldest Sully son in Avatar: The Way of Water

e.etymology: A recent American coinage that joins Win-, as in Winnie and Winslow, to the -sley ending of Kinsley and Ainsley.

e.meaning: wreath of flowers; or triangular piece of land
e.etymology: An English surname, either for a maker of garlands or from places named Garland, from Old English gara, a triangular strip of land. It was a fairly common American first name in the early 1900s.

assoc.t: Judy Garland, star of The Wizard of Oz

e.etymology: A 1990s American spelling of Alexis, from Greek alexein, to defend or help. The -us ending echoes the Lexus car brand, launched in 1989.
A less common spelling of Stephanie, the feminine of Stephen, from Greek stephanos, crown or garland. Stefani is also an Italian surname.

assoc.t: Gwen Stefani, No Doubt singer and TV coach

e.etymology: An English pet name built on the word love, used as a given name in the American South from the late 1800s.

e.meaning: bright sea (as a form of Muriel)
e.etymology: Usually taken as a variant of Muriel, from Gaelic muir, sea, and geal, bright; it has also been read as a blend of Mary and Beryl. Meryl Streep, born Mary Louise, made it famous.
An African-American coinage of the 1970s, close to Javon and to Jovan, the Serbian form of John.
The Polish feminine of Jan, the Polish John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. It is the Polish counterpart of Jane and Joanna.
A surname of Swiss German origin, common among Pennsylvania Mennonite families, used as a first name. Its best-known bearer was baseball's first commissioner, Kenesaw Mountain Landis.
The Spanish, Portuguese and Catalan form of Silvester, from Latin silvestris, wooded or of the forest. Pope Sylvester I's feast falls on New Year's Eve.
Taken from Raekwon, the stage name of Wu-Tang Clan rapper Corey Woods; boys were first given it in the mid-1990s as the group broke through. It follows the sound of Raequan and Daquan.
A modern name that blends Jared with Darren; also spelled Jaren and Jaron.
In Persian, Neda means voice or call, from Arabic nida. A separate South Slavic Neda is a short form of Nedeljka, from the word for Sunday.
